1. Tamil Nadu Development Model

  • Tamil Nadu's development achievement is based on a combination of:
  • Industrialisation.
  • Services.
  • Human-capital development.
  • Social welfare.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Social justice.
  • The State's development cannot be understood through economic growth alone.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Model → Economic Growth + Human Development + Social Justice

2. Growth and Welfare — Complementary Approach

  • Tamil Nadu's development experience combines industrial expansion with strong social policy.
  • Expenditure on education, health, nutrition and mobility can also strengthen productive capacity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Welfare + Human Capital → Can Support Economic Growth

3. Tamil Nadu GSDP — 2024–25

According to the supplied Economic Survey:

  • GSDP at current prices → approximately ₹31.19 lakh crore.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu GSDP 2024–25 → ₹31.19 Lakh Crore

4. Economic Growth — 2024–25

Tamil Nadu recorded:

  • Nominal growth → about 16%.
  • Real growth → 11.2%.

The supplied source identifies the 11.2% real growth as the highest among major States in 2024–25.

5. Contribution to India's Economy

  • Tamil Nadu contributed approximately 9.4% of India's GDP in 2024–25 according to the supplied source.
  • This was substantially higher than its share of India's population and geographical area.
📌 Must-Memorise

Small Territorial Share → Large National Economic Contribution

6. Per Capita Income — 2024–25

According to the supplied source:

  • Tamil Nadu → approximately ₹3.62 lakh.
  • India → approximately ₹2.05 lakh.
  • Tamil Nadu → about 1.77 times the national average.

7. Per Capita Income Ranking

⚠️ TNPSC Current-Fact Rule

Rankings should always be linked to the relevant year and dataset.

8. Broad-Based District Development

📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu's economy is not concentrated only in Chennai.

📌 Must-Memorise

57. Women's Employment — Unfinished Frontier

  • Barriers identified in the source include:
  • Care responsibilities.
  • Mobility.
  • Social norms.
  • Availability of quality jobs.
📌 Must-Memorise

Education Empowerment → Must Progress to Economic Empowerment

58. Balanced Growth, Sustainability and Future Direction

Tamil Nadu's achievements coexist with challenges involving:

  • Regional inequality.
  • Groundwater depletion.
  • Pollution.
  • Waste.
  • Climate change.
  • Urban infrastructure.
  • Fiscal pressures.
  • Employment quality.

Tamil Nadu's next development stage requires:

Sustainable

  • Inclusive
  • Employment-Rich Growth
📌 Must-Memorise

Achievement ≠ Completion of Development

59. TNPSC Traps

  • Tamil Nadu's development model is not based on one sector.
  • Economic growth and welfare are not necessarily contradictory.
  • Tamil Nadu GSDP in 2024–25 was approximately ₹31.19 lakh crore in the supplied source.
  • Nominal growth and real growth are different.
  • Real growth in 2024–25 → 11.2%.
  • Tamil Nadu's GDP contribution in the cited year → about 9.4% of India.
  • Per capita income → about ₹3.62 lakh in 2024–25.
  • High per capita income does not mean equal income distribution.
  • 32 of 38 districts above the national per capita income average does not mean all districts have identical income.
  • Tamil Nadu is a multi-centre economy, not a Chennai-only economy.
  • Manufacturing real growth → 14.74% in 2024–25.
  • Tamil Nadu's factory workforce share in the cited comparison → about 15%.
  • “Detroit of India” refers to Tamil Nadu's automobile ecosystem.
  • Tamil Nadu's industrial achievement includes both traditional and advanced manufacturing.
  • Merchandise exports almost doubled between 2020–21 and 2024–25.
  • Tamil Nadu ranked first in cited electronics, textiles and leather-product exports.
  • Total-export rank in the supplied source → 3rd, not 1st.
  • Export Preparedness Index rank → 2nd in the cited comparison.
  • FDI figures are year-specific and should not be treated as permanent rankings.
  • Investment announcements alone do not prove development impact.
  • Tamil Nadu ranked first in ragi and sugarcane yield in the cited 2024–25 data.
  • Gross cropped area and net sown area are different.
  • Livestock and fisheries are part of the rural economy.
  • MSMEs and large firms perform complementary roles.
  • Tiruppur → Knitwear.
  • Coimbatore → Engineering and textiles.
  • Chennai region → Automobiles and electronics.
  • Hosur → Advanced manufacturing.
  • All 38 districts being covered by industrial corridors does not mean equal industrialisation in every district.
  • Capital expenditure supports long-term productive assets.
  • Engineering-college count and polytechnic count are source-dated.
  • High higher-education GER does not automatically mean high educational quality or employability.
  • Female GER being high does not automatically mean high female labour-force participation.
  • NIRF rankings change every year.
  • IMR and MMR use different denominators.
  • IMR → per 1,000 live births.
  • MMR → per 100,000 live births.
  • TFR of 1.3 indicates advanced demographic transition but also creates future ageing challenges.
  • Life expectancy ranking is year- and dataset-specific.
  • MPI 2.20% and 1.43% are not directly interchangeable.
  • 2.20% → NITI Aayog 2019–21 MPI.
  • 1.43% → later State Economic Survey estimate for 2022–23.
  • Tamil Nadu's social-development outcomes cannot be attributed to reservation alone.
  • Welfare expenditure should be judged by outcomes, not merely spending.
  • Universal PDS is an important part of Tamil Nadu's food-security architecture.
  • Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation is part of the social-justice model, but social justice extends beyond reservation.
  • Women's education is an achievement, while women's employment remains an unfinished challenge.
  • Economic growth can coexist with regional inequality.
  • Strong development outcomes do not remove environmental and fiscal constraints.
  • Tamil Nadu's future goal should be sustainable and employment-rich growth, not growth alone.
  • The correct achievement chain is Industry + Services + Human Capital + Welfare + Infrastructure + Social Justice, not any one component in isolation.
